Q698842.title: 1860 United States presidential election
paras: The presidential election of 6 November 1860 was fought over slavery and was won by the Republican Abraham Lincoln of Illinois, with Hannibal Hamlin of Maine as his running mate. The Democratic president James Buchanan did not run again. The Republican platform promised not to interfere with slavery in the states where it existed but opposed its spread into the western territories, and also called for protective tariffs, free homesteads for settlers in the West and a railroad to the Pacific.

The parties split along sectional lines. At the Republican convention in Chicago in May, the front-runner was Senator William H. Seward of New York. Seward led on the first ballot, Lincoln's managers won over delegates (the Miller Center says with offers of cabinet posts to Indiana and Pennsylvania), and Lincoln won on the third ballot on 18 May. The Democratic convention in Charleston broke up when Southern delegates walked out over the party's slavery platform. When the party met again in Baltimore in June, Southern delegates walked out once more. The remaining Northern Democrats nominated Senator Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois, who wanted the settlers of each territory to decide on slavery. The bolters nominated Vice President John C. Breckinridge of Kentucky on a platform calling for federal protection of slavery in the territories. Former Whigs and Know Nothings formed the Constitutional Union Party and nominated John Bell of Tennessee, hoping to save the Union by avoiding the slavery question.

Following custom, Lincoln stayed at home in Springfield while Republican 'Wide Awake' clubs marched for him; only Douglas toured the country in person. Turnout was 81.2 percent, then the highest in American history. Lincoln carried the free states of the North and the Pacific coast and won 180 electoral votes, a clear majority, with just under 40 percent of the popular vote (39.7 percent according to Wikipedia, 39.8 according to the American Presidency Project). He received votes in only one of the eleven states that would later form the Confederacy, Virginia; the Miller Center says he was not on the ballot in any Southern state. Breckinridge won 72 electoral votes and eleven slave states, Bell 39 and three states of the upper South (Virginia, Kentucky and Tennessee), and Douglas, second in the popular vote, only 12 electoral votes, from Missouri and part of New Jersey.

Lincoln's victory without a single slave state ended the South's long hold over the federal government and became the main trigger of secession. Seven Southern states, all of which had voted for Breckinridge, left the Union before his inauguration on 4 March 1861. The Civil War began less than two months later with the attack on Fort Sumter, after which four more slave states seceded.

Q931982.title: Treaty of Fes
paras: The Treaty of Fes, signed on 30 March 1912 by Sultan Abd al-Hafid of Morocco and the French envoy Eugène Regnault, made Morocco a French protectorate. It ended more than half a century in which France, Britain, Spain and Germany competed for influence over the country, while debts, foreign loans and revolts weakened the sultan's government. By the Franco-British agreements of 1904 Britain left France a free hand in Morocco, and the Act of Algeciras of 1906 gave France and Spain control of Moroccan ports and police. Abd al-Hafid took the throne from his brother Abd al-Aziz in 1907–1908, but his authority kept collapsing.

Tribal forces in revolt then marched on Fes against the sultan, giving France the excuse to occupy Fes and Meknes. Germany's protest, a show of naval force off the Atlantic coast during the Agadir Crisis, was settled when it accepted France's position in Morocco in return for territory in the French Congo. That left the way open to a protectorate. Regnault, France's minister in Tangier, arrived in Fes on 24 March 1912 with the treaty text. On 29 March, with French troops around the city, he and the sultan negotiated for six hours at the royal palace, and the treaty was signed the next day. Wikipedia describes the sultan as signing under duress.

The treaty, modelled on the 1881 Treaty of Bardo for Tunisia, spoke of a 'new regime' of administrative, judicial, educational, financial and military reforms that France judged necessary, while promising to safeguard the sultan's traditional prestige and the practice of Islam. In practice a French resident-general held power over Morocco's foreign and internal affairs and alone could represent it abroad, while the sultan kept only the formal right to sign the decrees put before him.

The treaty was kept secret. When the people of Fes learned of it, and of the sultan's planned move to Rabat, the city rose on 17–19 April 1912; the French diplomatic archives estimate more than 700 victims, and Wikipedia records that the Jewish quarter was shelled by French artillery and then sacked. The resident-general Hubert Lyautey made Rabat the capital, and Abd al-Hafid soon abdicated in favour of his brother Yusuf. A Franco-Spanish treaty of 27 November 1912 created a Spanish zone in the north. Resistance went on in the Zaian and Rif wars, and the protectorate lasted until the Franco-Moroccan declaration of 2 March 1956 restored Morocco's independence.

Q934157.title: Battle of Ayacucho
Q934157.place: Pampa de Ayacucho (La Quinua), near Ayacucho (then Huamanga), Peru
paras: The Battle of Ayacucho, fought on 9 December 1824 on the Pampa de Ayacucho near the village of Quinua in the Peruvian Andes, was the decisive battle of the Peruvian War of Independence. The United Liberating Army, led by Simón Bolívar's lieutenant General Antonio José de Sucre and made up of Colombian and Peruvian units with Argentine and foreign volunteers, faced the royalist army of the Viceroy of Peru, José de la Serna, with General José de Canterac as his second in command. At the end of 1824 the royalists still held most of southern Peru and the fortress of Callao.

The Spanish side had been weakened from within. After the liberal revolution of 1820 Spain could send no reinforcements, and in early 1824 the royalist army of Upper Peru under Pedro Antonio Olañeta rebelled against the liberal viceroy after the restoration of absolute monarchy in Spain, tying down part of La Serna's forces. Bolívar beat Canterac at Junín in August, then left Sucre in command and went to Lima. On 3 December the royalists mauled Sucre's army at Corpahuaico (Matará), but Sucre kept it together. Short of food, the royalists took up a strong position on the heights of Condorcunca above the plain.

On the morning of the battle Canterac's plan was for the vanguard under Jerónimo Valdés to turn Sucre's left while the rest of the army came straight down the hillside. The descending units could not form up on the exposed slope, and José María Córdova's division, backed by William Miller's cavalry, broke them one after another; the royalist cavalry and the reserve, largely raw recruits, were also routed. By about one in the afternoon the wounded viceroy was a prisoner with many of his officers, and Valdés's men, who had been fighting La Mar's and Lara's divisions, fell back. The numbers differ by source. Wikipedia estimates about 5,780 patriots against 6,906 royalists on the day, while Sucre's letter to Bolívar, quoted by El Peruano, speaks of 6,000 men destroying 9,000. Wikipedia gives Sucre's figures of 370 patriots killed and 609 wounded and about 1,800 royalists dead and 700 wounded. The Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture gives 1,400 royalist dead and 700 wounded and about 900 patriot casualties.

Canterac, standing in for the captured viceroy, signed a capitulation with Sucre that same day. Under its terms the Spanish army handed over the territory it held in Peru up to the Desaguadero, together with Callao, and every Spanish soldier was free to go home at Peru's expense. Peru's official newspaper El Peruano calls the document Peru's real act of independence. Ayacucho ended Spanish power in South America, although Olañeta fought on in Upper Peru until April 1825 and the fortress of Callao held out until January 1826. Sucre went on to Upper Peru, which declared independence in August 1825 as the republic later named Bolivia, and he became its first president.

Q196502.title: Armistice of Cassibile
paras: The Armistice of Cassibile was Italy's surrender to the Allies in the Second World War, signed on 3 September 1943 at Cassibile near Syracuse in Allied-occupied Sicily. General Walter Bedell Smith, Eisenhower's chief of staff, signed for the Allies and Brigadier General Giuseppe Castellano for Italy, on behalf of Marshal Pietro Badoglio, head of the Italian government. King Victor Emmanuel III and Badoglio had approved it, but the signing was kept secret for five days.

By the summer of 1943 Italy was close to collapse. It had lost its African colonies, the Allies were bombing its cities, and Allied troops had landed in Sicily on 10 July. On 25 July the Fascist Grand Council adopted Dino Grandi's motion against Mussolini, the king dismissed him and had him arrested, and Badoglio became prime minister. Italy formally stayed Germany's ally while Hitler moved divisions south of the Alps, but Castellano made contact with the Allies in Lisbon. He then negotiated at Cassibile from 31 August, trying in vain to make the surrender depend on Allied landings strong enough to protect Rome from the Germans. On 1 September the king decided to accept the Allied terms.

The 'short armistice' that Castellano and Smith signed had twelve points. Italian forces were to stop all hostilities at once and deny the Germans anything that could be used against the Allies. Allied prisoners were to be handed over, and the fleet and aircraft sent where the Allies directed. Corsica and all Italian territory were to be put at the Allies' disposal as bases, and Italian forces were to withdraw from the war everywhere. Political, economic and financial conditions would follow later; this 'long armistice' was signed at Malta at the end of September. The date of the announcement was left to the Allies and tied to their landings. On 7 September Badoglio asked for a delay, saying his army could not support a planned American airborne landing at Rome, but Eisenhower kept to the date.

The armistice was broadcast on 8 September, by Eisenhower on Radio Algiers and by Badoglio on Italian radio; Il Post and the Liberation Route Europe portal put Eisenhower first, while Wikipedia has Badoglio speak first. Germany, which had expected the surrender, at once launched Operation Achse. Most Italian units had no orders and fell apart, and the Germans captured hundreds of thousands of Italian soldiers and occupied northern and central Italy and Rome. Early on 9 September the king, the royal family and Badoglio fled Rome for Brindisi, and the Allies landed at Salerno. Italian garrisons in Greece and the Balkans were overwhelmed, and on Cephalonia the Acqui Division was massacred after resisting. The fleet sailed to surrender to the Allies, losing the battleship Roma to German bombs on the way. On 12 September the Germans freed Mussolini, who set up the Italian Social Republic in the north, while an Italian resistance movement grew in occupied Italy.

Q1471139.title: Évian Accords
paras: The Évian Accords, concluded on 18 March 1962 at Évian-les-Bains on Lake Geneva, ended the Algerian War between France and the Algerian nationalists of the National Liberation Front (FLN), which had begun with the FLN's call for independence on 1 November 1954. The two sides were the French government of President Charles de Gaulle and the Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic (GPRA). The official French text names the FLN as the other party, as Paris never recognised the GPRA, while the Algerian text published in El Moudjahid names the GPRA.

De Gaulle, in power since 1958, accepted the principle of self-determination for Algeria in September 1959, and a referendum in January 1961 opened the way to talks. After talks at Melun near Paris failed in June 1960, Switzerland acted as go-between at the request of both sides: the Swiss diplomat Olivier Long passed on the first contacts, the Algerian delegates stayed in Switzerland, and the two sides met at Lucerne and Neuchâtel and then just across the border at Évian, Lugrin and Les Rousses. The Swiss Historical Dictionary calls this the most remarkable chapter of Swiss 'good offices' diplomacy. The final round at Évian ran from 7 to 18 March 1962.

The accords had two parts. A ceasefire ended all military operations and armed action throughout Algeria at noon on 19 March 1962. Government declarations then set out the transition. A provisional executive and a French high commissioner would govern until a referendum on self-determination, to be held within three to six months. Prisoners were to be released within 20 days and an amnesty declared. If Algeria chose independence, there were guarantees for people keeping French civil status, French troops would withdraw in stages, France kept the naval base of Mers el-Kébir on a 15-year lease along with other military facilities, and French companies kept their rights in Saharan oil and mining in return for French technical and financial aid.

French voters approved the accords in a referendum on 8 April 1962, by 17,866,423 votes to 1,809,074 according to Wikipedia. In Algeria the referendum of 1 July 1962 approved independence, which France recognised on 3 July; Algerians celebrated it on 5 July, ending 132 years of French rule. But peace did not come at once. The OAS, a secret army of opponents of independence, carried on its bombing campaign, and several hundred thousand Europeans left Algeria. Hundreds of Europeans were killed or abducted in Oran on 5 July, and thousands of harkis, Algerians who had served with the French army, were massacred despite the amnesty.

Q862054.title: Nixon's visit to China (1972)
paras: From 21 to 28 February 1972 President Richard Nixon visited the People's Republic of China, the first American president to visit mainland China while in office. He came at the invitation of Premier Zhou Enlai, accompanied by his wife Pat Nixon, Secretary of State William Rogers and National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger. Since the Communist victory of 1949 the United States had recognised only the Republic of China on Taiwan, and the two countries had no official relations.

Both sides had reasons to change this. The US Office of the Historian says that the Vietnam War led American officials to seek better relations with Communist governments in Asia, to isolate North Vietnam and gain leverage over the Soviet Union, while the Sino-Soviet split made Beijing look for a counterweight. Nixon eased travel and trade restrictions and opened a secret channel through Pakistan's President Yahya Khan, and China's foreign ministry notes that messages also passed through Romania. Beijing answered through the writer Edgar Snow and by inviting the American table tennis team in April 1971 ('ping-pong diplomacy'). Kissinger made a secret trip to Beijing in July 1971, and on 15 July Nixon announced on television that he would go to China.

Soon after his arrival in Beijing on 21 February, Nixon met Chairman Mao Zedong, the only meeting between the two during the visit, and he held long talks with Zhou Enlai. The party saw the Great Wall, Hangzhou and Shanghai, while Pat Nixon toured schools, hospitals and a commune before a large American press corps. The visit ended with the Shanghai Communiqué. The US text is dated 27 February, while China's foreign ministry dates the communiqué 28 February. In it both sides set out their differences openly. Both agreed to base their relations on peaceful coexistence and that neither would seek hegemony in the Asia-Pacific region. China called Taiwan the crucial obstacle to normal relations and a province of China. The United States 'acknowledged' that Chinese on both sides of the Taiwan Strait held that there was but one China, did not challenge that position, and promised to reduce its forces on Taiwan as tension eased.

Nixon called it 'the week that changed the world'. The visit shifted the Cold War balance and widened the rift between Moscow and Beijing. Taiwan saw it as a betrayal, and Japan and South Korea were shocked not to have been consulted. Within a year Japan, Australia and West Germany had broken relations with Taiwan in favour of Beijing. The principles of the Shanghai Communiqué became the basis for full diplomatic relations between the United States and the People's Republic, established in 1979.

Q4142069.title: Kazakh famine of 1930–1933
paras: The Kazakh famine of 1930–1933, in Kazakh Asharshylyq, was a man-made famine in Soviet Kazakhstan caused by Stalin's collectivisation of agriculture. Most of its victims were Kazakhs, a Muslim, Turkic-speaking people who made up roughly 60 percent of the republic's population and of whom many lived as pastoral nomads. They moved their sheep, horses and camels along seasonal routes across the steppe. In 1928 a grain shortage led Stalin to launch the first Five-Year Plan, and Soviet planners came to see nomadism as an obstacle to rapid industrialisation. Some argued that settling the Kazakhs would free large areas of the steppe for growing grain.

The 'war on nomadism' began in 1928 with the confiscation of the property of rich Kazakhs. It became full forced collectivisation in the winter of 1929–30 under the republic's party chief, Filipp Goloshchekin. Moscow declared that nomads were to be settled permanently and driven into collective farms, which had to deliver meat and grain to the state, and it left Kazakh activists in the auls (nomad camps) to decide who counted as an exploiter and how much to confiscate. According to the historian Sarah Cameron, many local cadres used the campaign to settle old scores, which made the violence worse. Herds collapsed: animals were slaughtered for food or sold to meet grain quotas, and those penned in collective farms died of disease and lack of fodder. Cameron says the republic lost about 90 percent of its livestock. Revolts broke out across the steppe, and by the winter of 1932–33 there was mass starvation, with epidemics and even cannibalism.

Hundreds of thousands fled to neighbouring Soviet republics and to China; Cameron puts the refugees at more than a million, about a fifth of the republic's population. The Soviet authorities closed the borders, and thousands were shot trying to cross into China. The toll is still disputed. Cameron estimates 1.5 million dead, about 1.3 million of them Kazakhs, roughly a third of all Kazakhs. The historian Nazira Nurtazina lists Kazakh and foreign estimates ranging from 1 million (Conquest) through 1.75 million, the figure most often cited, to over 2.1 million (the Kazakh demographer M. Tatimov).

The famine made Kazakhs a minority in their own republic; they regained a majority only after the Soviet collapse in 1991. Survivors were forced into a settled life, and Cameron argues that the catastrophe both created Soviet Kazakhstan as a fixed territory and replaced the old identity built on nomadism with a Kazakh national one. Kazakh researchers have called the famine 'Goloshchekin's genocide' or an 'ethnocide'. Cameron finds no evidence that Stalin planned it or meant to destroy all Kazakhs, but says it fits a broader definition of genocide. On 31 May Kazakhstan remembers the victims of political repression and of the famine.

Q25238182.title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
Q25238182.place: River Rubicon (Rubico), between Ravenna and Ariminum (Rimini), Italy
paras: In January 49 BC Julius Caesar led soldiers across the Rubicon (Latin Rubico), a small river in north-eastern Italy that marked the border between his province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy proper. A governor who brought an army across it was in effect invading his own country, so the crossing opened civil war between Caesar and the Senate, which looked to Pompey the Great for military leadership.

Caesar and Pompey had been allies with Marcus Crassus in the so-called First Triumvirate, but after the death of Caesar's daughter Julia, Pompey's wife, and of Crassus, the partnership fell apart. While Caesar conquered Gaul and won wealth and popularity, Pompey drew closer to the conservative senators who opposed Caesar. Caesar wanted to stand for a second consulship while keeping his army, and the tribunes on his side vetoed the attempts to make him give up his command. On 7 January 49 BC the Senate passed its emergency decree, the senatus consultum ultimum, against him, and the tribunes loyal to him fled Rome.

Caesar was waiting at Ravenna. According to Suetonius he sent a few cohorts ahead in secret, spent the day at a public show and a banquet to avoid suspicion, and left after sunset with a small party, catching up with his troops at the river. Ancient writers dramatised the moment. Suetonius describes Caesar hesitating until a supernatural figure seized a trumpet and crossed first, and Appian says he crossed 'like one inspired' with the words 'the die is cast', a line from Caesar's favourite poet, Menander. Appian adds that Caesar took Ariminum (Rimini) around daybreak. The Origins essay notes that these accounts were written long after the event and that Caesar had in fact already decided, since troops had been sent ahead to take Ariminum. It places the crossing three days after the Senate's decree.

Pompey and much of the Senate abandoned Rome as Caesar marched south. Caesar first defeated Pompey's forces in Spain, then crossed to Greece and beat Pompey himself at Pharsalus in August 48 BC. The war left Caesar effectively sole ruler of Rome and opened the way for his adopted son Octavian to become the first emperor. The exact site of the river is uncertain; Livius notes that the stream at Savignano long known as the Fiumicino was renamed after the Rubicon in 1933, following the distance given on the Peutinger map.

Q179975.title: Chinese Civil War
paras: The Chinese Civil War was fought, with long pauses, between the Nationalist government of the Republic of China, led by the Kuomintang (KMT) and Chiang Kai-shek, and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), from 1 August 1927 until the Communist victory of 1949. The two parties had first worked together in the First United Front: with Soviet help they fought the warlords who divided China, and in 1926–27 they carried out the Northern Expedition. But the alliance broke apart. On 12 April 1927 Communists were purged in Shanghai with hundreds of arrests and executions, the start of what the CCP calls the White Terror, and on 1 August 1927 the Communists rose at Nanchang, the founding act of their Red Army.

In the first phase the Nationalists, who took Beijing in 1928 and ruled most of eastern China from Nanjing, tried to destroy the Communist bases in the south in five encirclement campaigns. In October 1934 the Communists broke out and began the Long March, a year-long retreat of thousands of kilometres to Shaanxi in the north-west, during which Mao Zedong rose to lead the movement. Chiang kept fighting the Communists even after Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931. Then generals frustrated with this policy seized him in the Xi'an Incident and forced him to accept a Second United Front against Japan. Wikipedia places the incident in late 1936, while the US Office of the Historian gives 1937. During the war with Japan from 1937 to 1945 the truce was largely nominal and clashes continued. The Communists waged guerrilla war and built up their rural base and popular support, while corruption and repression weakened the Nationalist government.

After Japan's surrender both sides raced to take over the occupied areas. The United States flew Nationalist troops into them, while the Soviet Union, occupying Manchuria, let Communist forces move in behind it. Talks between Chiang and Mao at Chongqing in autumn 1945, and the mediation of the American general George Marshall, failed, and by 1946 full-scale war had resumed. The Communists drew landless peasants to their side with land reform and were helped by mass defections of Nationalist troops. In the three great campaigns of 1948–49, Liaoshen in Manchuria, Huaihai in east-central China and Pingjin around Beijing and Tianjin, they destroyed the Nationalist field armies; Wikipedia puts Nationalist losses through capture, surrender or defection at about 1.54 million men.

Communist troops took the Nationalist capital Nanjing on 23 April 1949, and on 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. The Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan on 7 December 1949, and the Communists completed their control of the mainland in 1950–51. Both sides committed mass atrocities: Wikipedia cites estimates that the Nationalists killed between 300,000 and one million people in the anti-communist campaigns after 1927. The war never formally ended. No armistice or peace treaty was signed, and the Republic of China on Taiwan and the People's Republic on the mainland both long claimed to be the legitimate government of all China. The 'loss' of China and the Korean War then kept the United States and the People's Republic apart for decades.

Q167634.title: Perestroika
paras: Perestroika ('restructuring') was the reform programme that Mikhail Gorbachev pursued as general secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1985 until 1991, together with glasnost ('openness'). Neither word was new to Soviet rhetoric, but in a speech of December 1984, a few months before he took power, Gorbachev named them as key themes alongside uskorenie ('acceleration'). The aim was not to abandon the planned economy but to make socialism work better and end the economic stagnation, political sclerosis and public discontent of the early 1980s.

In the first years, 1985–87, Gorbachev spoke of modifying central planning but changed little, and 'acceleration' soon fell by the wayside. More basic reforms followed. A Law on Individual Labour Activity of November 1986 allowed some private work by individuals and families. The Law on State Enterprise of July 1987 let state firms sell output beyond their state orders as they chose, made them cover their costs from their own revenue, and moved control from ministries to elected workers' collectives. Joint ventures with foreign investors were allowed from June 1987. The Law on Cooperatives of 26 May 1988 permitted privately run businesses for the first time since Lenin's New Economic Policy was abolished in 1928, and cooperative restaurants, hairdressers and repair shops soon flourished in the cities. Their higher prices and use of scarce state supplies made 'cooperative owner' a term of abuse.

Politically, Gorbachev came to call perestroika a 'revolution'. From January 1987 he appealed over the heads of the party for democratisation, with contested elections for the soviets and a new Congress of People's Deputies. In its election of March 1989, Soviet voters chose a national legislature for the first time and crossed many unopposed party officials off the ballot. Glasnost, meant to support reform, grew into a freedom of speech asserted from below. Lewis Siegelbaum, writing for the Seventeen Moments in Soviet History project, argues that its flood of revelations about crime and past state crimes undermined public confidence in the state.

The economic reforms did little to revive the economy. Price controls, the inconvertible rouble and most state control of production remained, and shortages deepened while the republics pressed for sovereignty. By the party congress of July 1990 it was clear that the reforms had sweeping unintended consequences. Perestroika is often counted among the main causes of the collapse of the Eastern Bloc and of the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991.

Q7968690.title: War of the Heavenly Horses
Q7968690.place: Ferghana Valley (Dayuan), reached from Dunhuang across the Tarim Basin
paras: The War of the Heavenly Horses was fought between Han China under Emperor Wu and Dayuan, a kingdom in the Ferghana Valley of Central Asia. Emperor Wu had heard of Dayuan's 'heavenly horses' from his envoy Zhang Qian and wanted them for the cavalry with which the Han fought the Xiongnu. He sent a mission with 1,000 pieces of gold and a golden horse to buy the best horses, which were kept at Ershi. Dayuan, already well stocked with Chinese goods and sure that China was too far away to send an army, refused. The envoys smashed the golden horse and left in anger, and the nobles of Dayuan had them killed and robbed at Yucheng on their eastern border.

In 104 BC the emperor sent Li Guangli, brother of his favourite concubine Lady Li, against Dayuan with the title 'Ershi General'. Wikipedia gives his army as 6,000 cavalry and 20,000 infantry; Friedrich Hirth's 1917 translation of the Han account gives 6,000 cavalry and 'several hundred thousand' recruits. Crossing the Tarim Basin, the army had to besiege oasis towns that refused it supplies, and it was worn down by hunger. Defeated at Yucheng, Li judged that he could not take Dayuan's capital and fell back to Dunhuang. The Han account says only one or two in ten of his soldiers were left, and that the angry emperor closed the Yumen Gate to the returning army, so Li stayed at Dunhuang.

Court officials wanted to give up the war and turn on the Xiongnu, but Emperor Wu feared losing prestige among the western states. Li set out again in 102 BC with 60,000 men, many of them convicts and young toughs, 30,000 horses and 100,000 oxen, this time well supplied. Most oasis states gave in; Luntai resisted and was destroyed. With about half his army left (30,000 men in the Han account), Li beat Dayuan's army in the field with his archers and crossbowmen, diverted the river that supplied the capital, which had no wells, and after a siege of more than forty days broke through the outer wall and captured the general Jianmi. A Wusun force of 2,000 horsemen, sent at the emperor's request, stayed out of the fighting.

The nobles in the inner city then killed their king, Wugua, sent his head to Li and offered horses and supplies if the Han withdrew, threatening to kill the horses otherwise. Li accepted. Hirth's translation says the Han took several dozen of the best horses and more than 3,000 lesser ones; Wikipedia says some 3,000 horses. Li made a noble friendly to the Han, Meicai, king and turned back. On the way home a detachment that attacked Yucheng was beaten, but Shangguan Jie then took the town, and its king, who had fled to Kangju, was handed over and killed. Only about 10,000 men and 1,000 horses came back through the Yumen Gate, mostly because officers had abused their men, yet the emperor rewarded the army and made Li Guangli Marquis of Haixi. The Han account says the whole campaign took four years.

The small states along the route sent princes to the Han court as hostages. More than a year after the war Dayuan's nobles killed Meicai and made Wugua's brother Chanfeng king; he sent a son to China as a hostage and the Han made peace with him. The Han guarded the road west towards Lop Nur with military posts and stationed soldier-farmers at Luntai, and Wikipedia says the war led smaller oasis states to turn from the Xiongnu to the Han, preparing the later Protectorate of the Western Regions.

Q134178.title: Minoan civilization
Q134178.place: Crete (Knossos, Phaistos, Malia, Zakros and other sites), with settlements and influence across the southern Aegean
paras: The Minoan civilization was the Bronze Age culture of Crete. Its name is modern: Arthur Evans popularised it from Minos, the mythical king whom the Classical Greeks placed at Knossos. What the Minoans called themselves is unknown; the Egyptians called them Keftiu. Wikipedia dates the culture's growth out of the island's Neolithic farming communities to about 3100 BC, at the start of the Early Bronze Age. Crete is poor in metals, and the Minoans traded farm produce and luxury crafts for them; by the Early Minoan II period their ships were reaching Egypt and Syria.

From about 2100 BC the populations of Knossos, Phaistos and Malia grew sharply, and the first palaces were built there in the period archaeologists call Middle Minoan IB (c. 1925-1875 BC in Wikipedia; ca. 2000/1950-1900/1850 BC in Jeremy Rutter's Dartmouth course, which counts only Knossos and Phaistos as certain palaces of that time). These large complexes held stores of farm produce and craft workshops, and are now thought to have had religious and economic roles rather than being royal homes. The Minoans developed two scripts, Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A, neither of which has been fully deciphered. After destructions at the end of the next period, new palaces were built at Knossos, Malia, Zakros and Kommos, opening the Neopalatial or 'New Palace' period (from c. 1750-1700 BC in Wikipedia, ca. 1750/1720 BC in the Dartmouth course).

In the Neopalatial age Minoan influence spread through the southern Aegean: its mark grew strong at island towns such as Akrotiri on Thera, Phylakopi on Melos and Ayia Irini on Keos, and Kastri on Kythera was a Minoan colony. The eruption of the Thera volcano, dated by carbon dating to around 1600 BC (Egyptian synchronisms put it about a century later; the Dartmouth course gives ca. 1625 BC), destroyed Akrotiri, but Knossos went on prospering. Then, at the end of Late Minoan IB (c. 1470 BC in Wikipedia, ca. 1490/1470 BC in the Dartmouth course), almost every Minoan site of note was destroyed, and the palaces of Phaistos, Malia and Zakros were never rebuilt as palaces. The cause is still argued over: Mycenaean invaders, internal unrest, earthquakes or the after-effects of the eruption have all been proposed.

Knossos alone stayed in use as a palace. Who ruled it is debated: the Dartmouth course lists a Mycenaean conqueror, his viceroy, or a Minoan ruler backed by Mycenaean soldiers. The palace's records came to be kept in Linear B, a script adapted from Linear A to write Mycenaean Greek, which shows that a Greek-speaking elite now ran the administration; Linear B was deciphered in 1952. The Dartmouth course dates a great fire at Knossos to ca. 1385/1375 BC, after which Crete split among regional centres such as Ayia Triadha and Chania. From about 1200 BC, during the wider Late Bronze Age collapse, coastal settlements were abandoned for defensible hilltops, and this hybrid Minoan-Mycenaean culture faded out around 1100 BC.

The Minoans were then largely forgotten until excavations in the early 20th century, led at Knossos by Arthur Evans, brought them back to light. In July 2025 the British School at Athens reported that Knossos had joined the UNESCO World Heritage List together with the palaces of Phaistos, Malia, Zakros, Zominthos and Kydonia.

Q715380.title: First Triumvirate
Q715380.place: Rome; renewed in 56 BC at Ravenna and Luca (Lucca) in Cisalpine Gaul
paras: The 'First Triumvirate' was an informal and at first secret alliance of three leading Roman politicians: Pompey, Marcus Licinius Crassus and Julius Caesar. The name is modern. It was not an office, and contemporaries described it in other ways: Cicero wrote of 'three men' holding a kind of kingship, and Varro called it a 'three-headed monster'. Each man had been blocked by opponents in the Senate, led by Cato and Metellus Celer. Pompey wanted his settlement of the East after the Third Mithridatic War ratified and land for his veterans. Crassus wanted relief for the tax-farming companies of Asia, which had bid too much for their contracts. Caesar, back from Spain in 60 BC, gave up his claim to a triumph in order to stand for the consulship of 59, and his opponents secured the election of a hostile colleague, Bibulus.

Caesar brought together the old rivals Pompey and Crassus. The ancient writers disagree on whether the pact came before or after his election, and Wikipedia places it between July 60 and January 59 BC. As consul in 59, Caesar proposed a land law that would settle Pompey's veterans. When Cato obstructed it in the Senate, Caesar took it to the people, with Pompey and Crassus at his side; Pompey promised to answer swords with a shield. Bibulus was driven from the forum and later shut himself up at home. Laws followed that ratified Pompey's eastern settlement and cut the tax farmers' debts by a third. Pompey married Caesar's daughter Julia, and Caesar received Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum for five years, to which the Senate added Transalpine Gaul.

The alliance's strong-arm methods made it unpopular, and it frayed while Caesar campaigned in Gaul and the tribune Clodius turned against Pompey. In 56 BC Caesar met Crassus at Ravenna and Pompey at Luca, where some two hundred senators came to pay court. The pact was renewed: Pompey and Crassus were elected consuls again for 55 BC after violence and bribery, Caesar's command was extended for another five years, and a law of the tribune Trebonius gave Crassus Syria and Pompey the Spanish provinces for five years.

Julia died in childbirth in 54 BC, and in 53 BC Crassus was killed by the Parthians at Carrhae. Wikipedia notes that modern scholars no longer simply accept the ancient view that Julia's death made a clash inevitable, but Crassus's death turned the three-way alliance into a rivalry between two men. Pompey built ties with Caesar's opponents and became sole consul in 52 BC, and in January 49 BC Caesar went into open rebellion. Plutarch judged that it was not the quarrel between Caesar and Pompey that brought on the civil wars, but their friendship.

Q212079.title: Second Triumvirate
Q212079.place: Agreed on an island in a river near Mutina (Modena); made law in Rome
paras: The Second Triumvirate was a legal commission that gave three Caesarian leaders, Mark Antony, Lepidus and Caesar's adopted heir Octavian, almost absolute power over the Roman state. After Julius Caesar's murder on 15 March 44 BC, Antony and Octavian fell out. Urged on by Cicero, the Senate turned against Antony, whose forces were put to flight at Mutina on 21 April 43 BC, and he was declared a public enemy. With both consuls dead, Octavian marched on Rome, became consul in August 43 BC, had the decree against Antony repealed, and moved north to make terms with him under Lepidus's protection.

The three men met on a small island in a river near Mutina; Appian says Octavian and Antony each brought five legions, which faced each other across the river, and the three conferred for two days. They agreed on a new office, to be held for five years with powers above the consuls', and split the western provinces: Antony took Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul, Lepidus Narbonese Gaul and Spain, and Octavian Africa, Sardinia and Sicily. They promised their soldiers the land of eighteen rich Italian towns. In Rome a tribune, Publius Titius, carried the law at once (the lex Titia), and Wikipedia dates its formal creation to 27 November 43 BC. The triumvirs could issue binding edicts, overrule governors, punish without right of appeal and appoint the magistrates.

They began with proscriptions: lists of men to be killed and their property sold, with rewards for killers and informers. Cicero, who had attacked Antony in his speeches, was among the victims, and his head and hand were put on show in the Forum. The ancient numbers differ. Appian names 17 first and then 130 and 150 more, and gives about 300 senators and 2,000 knights condemned; Wikipedia notes that this total covers everyone killed or stripped of property up to 39 BC, while Plutarch gives between 200 and 300 and Livy 130 senators besides many knights.

In 42 BC Antony and Octavian took their armies to Macedonia against Caesar's assassins. In two battles at Philippi they defeated Brutus and Cassius, both of whom took their own lives, the second battle being fought on 23 October 42 BC. Afterwards Antony took charge of the East and Octavian of the West, and Lepidus was left with Africa. The triumvirate was renewed in 37 BC for five more years; in 36 BC Octavian forced Lepidus out, and the two remaining triumvirs fought a final war, from which Octavian emerged the victor.

Q202311.title: Roman Egypt
paras: Roman Egypt was the province of Aegyptus, which covered most of modern Egypt except Sinai from the Roman conquest in 30 BC until AD 642. The last Ptolemaic ruler, Cleopatra VII, had backed Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony. After Octavian won the naval battle of Actium he invaded Egypt, and at Alexandria in 30 BC Antony, then Cleopatra, killed themselves. Octavian took Egypt as his own possession; in his Res Gestae he wrote simply, 'Egypt I added to the empire of the Roman people.' According to Wikipedia its legal status was settled in 27 BC, when he received the name Augustus and Egypt became an imperial province.

Egypt was run differently from other provinces. Its governor, the prefect, was chosen by the emperor from the equestrian order rather than the Senate, and its legions were also commanded by equestrians, so that no governor could build up a rival power base as Antony had. Strabo, describing the province in his own day, says the prefect held the rank of the old kings, with a chief judge and an official who claimed ownerless property for Caesar under him, and that three legions and nine cohorts guarded the country, three of the cohorts at Syene on the Ethiopian border. The garrison was cut to two legions under Tiberius. Egypt paid considerable tribute and became a major grain producer for the empire, by far its richest province outside Italy, and Alexandria was its largest port and second city.

Most Egyptians were village farmers who spoke Egyptian, while the citizens of the nome capitals spoke Greek and lived a Hellenistic life; in AD 212 the Constitutio Antoniniana made all free Egyptians Roman citizens. In 269 the Palmyrene queen Zenobia took Egypt, and Aurelian won it back. Diocletian, who recovered the province from usurpers in 297-298, reformed its government and drew the southern frontier back to the First Cataract at Syene (Aswan). In the early 4th century Egypt was divided into smaller provinces. After Constantine took Egypt in 324 the emperors promoted Christianity, and Coptic emerged as the language of Egypt's Christians.

The Justinianic plague first appeared at Pelusium in Egypt in 541. The Sasanian Persians conquered Egypt in 618 and held it for a decade until it returned to the Eastern Roman Empire in 628. Roman rule ended in 642, when Egypt passed to the Rashidun Caliphate after the Muslim conquest.

Q4817850.title: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
Q4817850.place: Transoxiana, the lands beyond the Oxus (Amu Darya): Tokharistan, Sogdia (Bukhara, Samarkand), Khwarazm and the Jaxartes valley; base at Merv in Khorasan
paras: The Arab conquest of Transoxiana, 'the land beyond the river' Oxus (today parts of Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan), took about a century, from the first raids after Merv fell in 651 to the battle of Talas in 751. Wikipedia calls it the longest and hardest-fought of the early Muslim conquests. The region was split into many small principalities, in Tokharistan on the upper Oxus, in Sogdia around Bukhara and Samarkand, in Khwarazm and along the Jaxartes, with Iranian-speaking townspeople and mostly nomadic Turks.

At first the Arabs only raided for booty and tribute. The Umayyad governor Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan turned Khorasan into a base: he settled 50,000 warriors from Basra and Kufa with their families there (50,000 families in Gibb's account). His son Ubayd Allah reached Merv as governor in the autumn of 673 and the next spring crossed the Oxus, beat the Bukharans near Paykand and made Bukhara tributary, taking Bukharan archers back as his guard. In 676 Sa'id ibn Uthman defeated the Sogdians and took young nobles as hostages (50 in Gibb; Wikipedia says 40, 50 or 80). Then the Second Fitna, a new Muslim civil war, halted expansion for a generation while the Arab tribes of Khorasan fought each other.

The real conquest was the work of Qutayba ibn Muslim, governor from 705 under al-Hajjaj. He recovered Balkh and Lower Tokharistan in 705 and fought for Bukhara from 706 to 709, punishing rebellious Paykand by killing its men and enslaving its women and children. He then subdued Khwarazm and Samarkand, whose ruler Ghurak had to accept an Arab garrison and a mosque, and from 713 campaigned along the Jaxartes. Unlike earlier governors he enlisted large numbers of local troops. After the caliph al-Walid died in 715 Qutayba lost his life: Gibb says he was killed in a mutiny of his own army in Ferghana, while Wikipedia says the new caliph Sulayman most likely had him executed. A story that he reached Kashgar is rejected by Gibb and by the modern historians Wikipedia cites.

From 720 the Turgesh Turks, together with Sogdian uprisings, drove the Arabs back. On the 'Day of Thirst' in 724 only a handful of an Arab army reached Samarkand, and the Turgesh khagan Suluk took Bukhara in 728. Costly expeditions restored Arab authority at Samarkand by 732, Suluk was defeated at Kharistan in 737, and the governor Nasr ibn Sayyar had recovered most of Transoxiana by 743.

In July 751, by Gibb's dating, an Abbasid army under Ziyad ibn Salih defeated the Tang Chinese general Gao Xianzhi on the Talas after the Karluk Turks deserted the Chinese. This ended the Tang advance in the region, though Gibb argues that the real blow to Chinese prestige came in 757, when Central Asian contingents helped restore the Tang emperor to his capital and saw China's weakness. Islam spread slowly under the Umayyads, who did not encourage conversion, and much faster under the Abbasids, when converts gained equal status.
